hints.title: Keep the integer choices flexible
hints.body: The AP sum is n[2a+(n−1)d]2=20. The conditions ask what must hold in every integer AP with that total, so separate counterexamples may defeat separate claims.
hints.recap: One successful example does not force a parity rule.
hints.pitfall: The question does not say that n, a or d must be even.
hints.pause: Try short arithmetic progressions whose sum is 20.

recall.reminder: A single permitted counterexample disproves a universal claim.

hints.title: Explore a two-term progression
hints.body: An integer arithmetic progression with two terms has sum equal to those two terms. Try to make its first term odd while keeping the required total.
hints.recap: One valid progression can refute a claim about all such progressions.
hints.pitfall: Its common difference must also be an integer.
hints.pause: Check what this example says about statement I.

recall.reminder: One valid progression can refute a claim about all such progressions.

hints.title: Explore an odd number of terms
hints.body: Use the sum formula with an odd number of terms and an odd common difference. Solve for the first term and check that it is an integer.
hints.recap: Different claims may need different counterexamples.
hints.pitfall: Verify the sum instead of relying only on the parity of the chosen parameters.
hints.pause: Build a valid example and decide whether statements II and III are forced.

recall.reminder: Different claims may need different counterexamples.

solution:
The AP 9,11 consists of integers and sums to 20, but begins with an odd term. Therefore I need not be true.

The AP 2,3,4,5,6 has five terms and common difference 1; its sum is 5(2+6)2=20. Thus both its term count and common difference are odd, disproving II and III.

These examples satisfy every stated assumption, and the claims need not be refuted by the same example.

Answer A: none of them.
knowledgePattern: Refute parity claims using integer APs with a fixed total
